title: The Anatomy of a Strong Prompt

thumbnail.headline: Same Tool, Better Prompt
thumbnail.image: Navy background, two generated coffee cup images side by side: a flat grey one on the left and a warm café shot with blue-and-white tiles on the right, headline in teal Inter Bold.

slide.title: Same Tool, Better Prompt
slide.body: Left: plain generated cup on grey, labelled 'a coffee cup'. Right: warm generated café cup with gold rim and tiles. Small tag: AI Image Generation · Lesson 2.

production_notes: [VERSION] Gemini and Google AI Studio availability and free-tier image limits must be checked against the live tools before generating the example images.
Both coffee cup images on slides are generated in Gemini by the team from the two prompts shown. No logos, real café names or people in the images.
Scene 11 shows Inês's full rewritten prompt on a code slide; the voiceover only summarises it, so hold the slide long enough to read.
Inês and her Lisbon café are fictional; stock footage must not show a real café name or logo.
No hero B-roll: generated example images on slides carry the visuals.

Hook.voiceover: Two people type a coffee cup into the same tool. One gets a flat, forgettable picture. The other gets a warm image that could go on a café menu tomorrow. The tool is the same. The difference is the prompt.

Explain.voiceover: In the last lesson, you saw that anything you do not describe is filled in by the model, often differently each time. A strong prompt reduces this guessing. It tells the model what matters to you.

slide.title: The Anatomy of a Strong Prompt
slide.body: AI Image Generation and Visual Design · Lesson 2 of 12

Explain.voiceover: A simple formula helps you remember what to include. Subject, action, setting, style, composition, lighting and colour. Read it as a checklist, not as a rule you must follow in exact order.

slide.title: The prompt formula
slide.body: Seven labelled blocks in a row, each a different colour: Subject · Action · Setting · Style · Composition · Lighting · Colour. Caption: a checklist, not a strict order.

Explain.voiceover: Here is each part for a cup of coffee. The subject is a white ceramic cup. The action is steam rising. The setting is a marble café counter. The style is a product photograph. Each part answers one simple question about the picture.

slide.title: The formula in action, part 1
slide.body: Subject: a white ceramic coffee cup · Action: steam rising from the coffee · Setting: on a marble café counter · Style: product photograph

Explain.voiceover: The composition is a close-up from slightly above. The lighting is soft morning light from a window. And the colour is warm browns and cream. You do not need all seven every time. A quick idea may need three parts. A picture for a client usually needs all of them.

slide.title: The formula in action, part 2
slide.body: Composition: close-up, seen from slightly above · Lighting: soft morning light from a window on the right · Colour: warm browns and cream, one small touch of blue. Footer: quick idea = 3 parts · client image = all 7

Explain.voiceover: Think of a prompt as instructions for a taxi driver in a city they do not know. Take me to the centre gets you somewhere. Take me to the north entrance of the central station, near the bus stop, gets you to the right door. Each extra detail removes one wrong destination.
Explain.stock_query: taxi driver listening to passenger directions
Explain.on_screen_text: Each detail removes a wrong destination

Explain.voiceover: Specific words beat long lists of adjectives. Beginners often add words like beautiful, stunning or high quality. But these words do not tell the model anything it can draw. Compare a beautiful cup with a cup with a thin gold rim. The second phrase gives the model something it can show.

slide.title: Specific beats stunning
slide.body: Left, crossed out: 'beautiful, stunning, amazing, high quality'. Right, ticked: 'a cup with a thin gold rim' with a small generated close-up of the gold rim. Caption: replace praise words with visible details.

Explain.voiceover: So replace praise words with visible details. A material, a shape, a light direction, a colour. And keep the language plain, in short phrases or sentences. Most tools handle natural language well, so you do not need special codes.
Explain.on_screen_text: Describe what the viewer can see

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's see the formula at work. Inês owns a small café in Lisbon, Portugal. She wants a photo-style image for her online menu. Her first prompt is just three words: a coffee cup.
The result is a plain cup on a grey background. It could belong to any café in the world. So she uses the formula to rewrite it.

slide.title: Before
slide.body: Prompt in a code box: 'A coffee cup'. Next to it, the generated result: a plain cup on a flat grey background. Label: 'Could be any café'.

Demonstrate.voiceover: You can read her new prompt on screen. In short, she asks for a white cup with a thin gold rim and light steam, on a pale marble counter, with custard tarts behind it. It is a close-up product photograph from slightly above, with the cup in the left third, soft morning window light, and warm cream and brown tones with a blue and white tile pattern.

slide.title: After: Inês's rewritten prompt
slide.body:
A white ceramic cup of coffee with a thin gold rim, light steam rising,
on a pale marble café counter with a small plate of custard tarts behind it,
product photograph, close-up from slightly above, cup in the left third,
soft morning light from a window on the right,
warm cream and brown tones with a small blue-and-white tile pattern in the background
(each line tagged in the margin: subject/action · setting · style/composition · lighting · colour)

Demonstrate.voiceover: Now the image looks like it belongs to her café. The tiles suggest Lisbon. The light feels like early morning. And there is empty space on the right, where she can add the price later in a design tool. Notice what she did not write. No amazing, and no masterpiece. Every word describes something the viewer can see.

slide.title: After
slide.body: The generated rewritten image, with three callouts: 'tiles suggest Lisbon', 'morning window light', 'empty space for the price'.

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to fix a weak result by adding more and more words. Soon the prompt is long, and details start to fight, like dark moody lighting and bright sunny day. Instead, find the part of the formula that caused the problem, and change only that part. Then generate again and compare. Changing one thing at a time shows you what each word does.

slide.title: Change one part at a time
slide.body: Left, red: a long prompt with 'dark moody lighting' and 'bright sunny day' highlighted as a clash. Right, green: the formula blocks with only the Lighting block swapped, arrow to 'generate and compare'.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, a strong prompt covers subject, action, setting, style, composition, lighting and colour, as the task needs. Second, visible details like materials, angles and light direction work better than praise words. Third, when a result is wrong, change one part at a time and compare.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Use the formula: subject · action · setting · style · composition · lighting · colour. 2. Visible details beat praise words. 3. Fix one part at a time, then compare.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below, you will rewrite three weak prompts with the formula, generate both versions in Gemini, and compare them side by side. It takes about twenty minutes. In the next lesson, you will make your first images in Gemini and Firefly. See you there.
